name: PT Delta Giri Wacana Tbk

frontmatter.title: Delta Giri Wacana: growth in the field, a premium in the price
frontmatter.summary: Delta Giri Wacana sells pesticides and fertilizer to Indonesian farmers through a growing kiosk network, and management plans IDR4,880bn of revenue for the year. We initiate at ADD with a Rp287 target, 13.5% away: the business is growing, but the shares already trade at 1.04x the probability-weighted fundamental value today and the konglo lens keeps only part of that premium.
thesis: The distribution network is the asset: more than 20 warehouses and about 7,000 kiosks reach more than 10m farmers, and the company presents itself as a market leader in both pesticides and fertilizer [S7, S4, F71, F72, F73].

Growth is volume-led: FY2025 revenue rose 22.9% to IDR4,147.3bn on fertilizer volumes up 33.0% and pesticide volumes up 27.0%, and nine-month revenue is already IDR3,721.6bn [S3, S4, S2, F19, F38, F39].

Growth consumes cash: FY2025 operating cash flow was an outflow of IDR25.0bn against parent profit of IDR218.8bn, and the nine-month outflow was IDR401.2bn as inventories reached IDR2,390.1bn [S3, S2, F74, F17, F12].
The methods disagree by design: the discounted cash flow gives Rp238 a share, the peer EV/EBITDA cross-check Rp219 and the peer P/E Rp310; the blend of Rp244 sits below the Rp262 price [S0, S3].

What moves the target is the konglo lens, not a better forecast: DGWG is on the exchange HSC list and the public float is below the minimum, so the lens keeps part of the price-to-value gap and the target lands above the market on the base closure share [S11, S10, S9].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Delta Giri Wacana at ADD with a twelve-month target of Rp287, 13.5% from the Rp262 price. The company makes and distributes the inputs Indonesian farmers buy every season — pesticides, fertilizer, plastic mulch and sprayers — and sells them through more than 20 warehouses and about 7,000 kiosks that reach more than 10m farmers [S7, F71, F72, F73]. FY2025 revenue was IDR4,147.3bn and parent profit IDR218.8bn [S3]; the nine months to September 2026 had already produced IDR3,721.6bn of revenue, after first-half growth of 46.0% [S2, F19, F70]. Management raised its own revenue plan to IDR4,880.0bn after the first half [S5], and the forecast here takes that plan.

The business is growing and the shares have anticipated it. At Rp262 the market values the equity at 1.04x the probability-weighted fundamental value today of Rp251, and at a discount to the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp279 [S0]. The methods disagree in an informative way. The discounted cash flow, which charges the working capital the growth consumes, gives Rp238 a share; the peer EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp219; the peer P/E cross-check, which capitalises accounting profit without that cash charge, gives Rp310 [S0, S3]. Weighted at 60.0%, 25.0% and 15.0%, the fundamental value is Rp244, and the twelve-month value before the regime step is Rp279.

We do not bend those numbers toward the price. What closes the distance to the target is the konglo lens, applied because DGWG is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S11]. The controller holds 72.3% and the public float is 14.9%, below the exchange's raised minimum, with the deadline for issuers of this size in 2029 [S10, F40, F41]. A thin float in a regime that is removing HSC names from the benchmark [S9] is a flow story, not an earnings story. The lens assumes only 35.0% of the price-to-value gap closes over twelve months, which lifts the target to Rp287, 13.5% from the Rp262 price including the modelled dividend, and the rating is ADD.

An agro-input distributor sits between chemical and fertilizer manufacturers and the kiosks where
farmers buy. The products are seasonal, sold on credit into a harvest cycle, and the distributor
carries the inventory and the receivables between the factory gate and the farm. Scale comes from
the density of the kiosk network and from the working capital to hold stock through the planting
season; the margin is a spread over imported raw materials, and the risk is that the season is
late or the rupiah moves before the stock is sold.

What moves the value is therefore not the revenue line, which is well supported by the plan and the nine-month run-rate. It is the working-capital ratio, which decides how much of that revenue becomes cash; the fertilizer share of the mix, which decides the margin; and the float and index regime, which decides how much of the premium survives the next year. On our numbers the most likely path lands at Rp287, 9.7% above the Rp262 price before the dividend and 13.5% with it, which is why the rating is ADD.

Delta Giri Wacana is an Indonesian agro-input group: it manufactures and distributes crop-protection chemicals, fertilizer and farm equipment, and it sells through distributors, kiosks, plantation estates and government procurement [S4]. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in January 2025, selling new shares to fund working capital and the expansion of its pesticide and fertilizer capacity; the offering was sized to raise up to about a trillion rupiah at the top of its bookbuilding range [S7]. The controlling shareholder is David Yaory, who holds 72.3% of the shares, and the public holds 14.9% [S4, F40, F41]. The share count is 5,882m [S2, F43].

The revenue base is four reported segments. In FY2025 the pesticide segment produced IDR1,369.6bn of net revenue, fertilizer IDR2,599.8bn, farm equipment IDR77.2bn and distribution IDR1,137.7bn; the segments sum to more than consolidated revenue because intra-group sales are eliminated on consolidation [S3, F30, F31, F32, F33]. The consolidated revenue was IDR4,147.3bn [S3, F65]. Fertilizer is the larger segment by revenue and the lower-margin one; pesticides carry the brand and the formulation know-how; distribution is the channel that the other three use [S3, S4].

The channel is the strategic asset. The group operates more than 20 warehouses across the archipelago and works with about 7,000 partner kiosks, which the company says brings its products to more than 10m farmers, or roughly a third of Indonesia's farmers [S7, F71, F72, F73]. That reach is what a new entrant would have to build, and it is why the group describes itself as a market leader in pesticides and fertilizer rather than as one supplier among many [S7]. The channel is also where the working capital sits: inventory and receivables are carried through the season and collected after harvest [S2, S3].

On the manufacturing side the group runs a fertilizer plant with 300,000 tonnes of annual capacity, which produced 268,949 tonnes in FY2025 — the annual report puts that at about four-fifths of capacity [S4, F34, F35] — and a pesticide formulation operation that also buys finished product from third parties [S4]. In July 2025 the group inaugurated an agrochemical active-ingredient plant at Cikande in Banten, through its subsidiary PT Dharma Guna Wibawa, and has since exported carbamate active ingredient to South Africa [S4]. The plant moves part of the pesticide cost base from imported intermediate to domestic conversion, which is the main operational change since the listing [S4].

The sales are seasonal and credit-funded. Fertilizer volume was 513m kilograms in FY2025, up 33.0%, and pesticide volume was 18m units, up 27.0%; revenue rose 22.9% over the same year, which means realised prices per unit fell as cheaper inventory was sold through [S3, S4, F36, F37, F38, F39, F69]. That is the economics of a distributor in a deflationary input year: volume growth is easy to report, price is not. The customer base is the kiosk network and the plantation estates, and the government is a buyer through the subsidized fertilizer programme [S4].

Crop-protection products are sold on efficacy and on trust in the brand, because a farmer who buys a
counterfeit or a mis-dosed product loses a season. Registration of an active ingredient, labelling
and safe-use rules are administered, so the product range is slow to change and incumbents with a
registered portfolio have an advantage. Fertilizer is closer to a commodity: the brand matters less
than the analysis, the delivery date and the credit terms, and the subsidized segment is priced by
policy rather than by the market.

The addressable market is large and growing at a mid-single-digit rate in rupiah terms. Indonesian pesticide consumption is put at 21 trillion rupiah for 2026, growing 7.3%, and is forecast to reach 26 trillion by 2030, a compound rate of 6.3% [S4, F50, F51, F54, F55]. The premium fertilizer market is larger again at 131 trillion rupiah and growing 9.5%, of which the agricultural application segment is 88 trillion [S4, F52, F53, F56]. Against that, subsidized fertilizer consumption averages 9m tonnes a year against national production capacity of 15m tonnes, so the subsidized pool is allocated rather than sold [S4, F57, F58]. The growth rates in the source matter for the forecast: a distributor growing faster than the market is taking share, and one growing at the market rate is not.

For a distributor, the binding constraint is not demand but the cost of carrying the season. Input prices are set abroad: potash supply is concentrated in Canada, Russia and Belarus, which account for about 70.0% of the global market, and the fertilizer basket is imported in dollars [S4, F59]. Pesticide intermediates are petrochemical derivatives, so Brent is the second channel [S3, S4]. The company reports in rupiah and buys in dollars, and bank facilities were repriced to between 7.8% and 9.0% in July 2026 [S2, F63, F64]. The macro deck carries Brent at 96 and the rupiah at 17,570 for the year, against a spot rate of 18,140 [S0].

Demand is driven by planted area, the monsoon and farm incomes. The company attributes its 2026 growth to a favourable planting season, government programmes and stimulus in agriculture, and to its own inventory management through the input-cost cycle [S6]. The 2023 season is the counter-example: El Nino cut the agro-input business, and the company's first-half 2024 revenue and profit were depressed by it [S7]. Weather is therefore a first-order variable for revenue and for the inventory that sits behind it, and it is the reason the business is seasonal rather than smooth [S7, S6].

Competition is fragmented at the kiosk level and concentrated at the manufacturer and importer level. The group presents itself as one of the market leaders in pesticides and fertilizer [S7]; its advantage is the channel it owns or partners with, the registered product portfolio, and the ability to fund inventory through the season [S4]. The barriers are working capital and relationships rather than patents: a competitor with cheaper credit can buy shelf space, and a kiosk can switch supplier between seasons [S4, S7]. That is a narrow moat, and it is why we treat the share gains in the plan as something to be earned each year rather than as a stock of advantage.

The five forces are mixed. Buyer power is moderate: the kiosks are small and numerous, but the subsidized programme gives government procurement countervailing power on the fertilizer side [S4]. Supplier power is high on imported raw materials, where a handful of countries dominate potash [S4, F59]. The threat of new entrants is low at the formulation and registration level and higher in plain distribution, where the constraint is capital rather than know-how [S4]. Substitution is low in crop protection and high in fertilizer, where subsidized product competes with premium product on price [S4]. Rivalry is intense in the subsidized segment and brand-led in pesticides, which is why the mix shift toward fertilizer in FY2025 lowered the group margin [S3, F30, F31].

Indonesian agriculture is dominated by smallholders who buy inputs season to season, often on credit
from the kiosk, which in turn buys on credit from the distributor. The chain is therefore a chain of
receivables, and its health depends on the harvest and on the price of the crop the farmer sells.
Policy runs through the subsidized fertilizer allocation, which sets volumes and prices for a large
part of the market, and through food-security spending, which can lift demand quickly but is
budget-dependent.

Revenue grew from IDR1,687.2bn in FY2022 to IDR3,039.8bn and IDR3,373.1bn before reaching IDR4,147.3bn in FY2025 [S0, S3]. The path is not smooth: FY2023 was the El Nino year, when parent profit fell to IDR15.2bn despite the growth in the revenue base [S0, S7]. The recovery came through volume. Fertilizer and pesticide volumes rose by between a quarter and a third in FY2025 [S4, F38, F39], revenue rose 22.9% [S3, F69], and parent profit reached IDR218.8bn on a gross margin of 26.9% [S3].

The margin has stepped down as the mix has shifted. Gross margin was 22.6% in FY2022 and 23.1% in FY2023, rose to 27.6% in FY2024 and 26.9% in FY2025 [S0, S3]. The FY2025 number reflects a fertilizer segment that is now the larger part of net revenue and carries a lower gross margin than pesticides; the segment note discloses segment revenue and one elimination line only, so the two segment margins are our derivation from the consolidated cost of goods sold and the mix, not a reported split [S3, F30, F31]. Operating expenses were IDR713.2bn, or about a sixth of revenue, and the group's depreciation and amortisation was IDR57.8bn — materially above the data pack's figure, which is why we restate it [S3, p.109, F1, F67, F65].

The nine months to September 2026 show the growth and its cost. Revenue was IDR3,721.6bn and gross profit IDR926.4bn, a gross margin just under a quarter, with parent profit of IDR159.9bn, finance costs of IDR85.3bn and a tax charge of IDR51.0bn [S2, F19, F21, F20, F22, F24]. Operating cash flow was an outflow of IDR401.2bn [S2, F17], driven by inventories of IDR2,390.1bn and trade receivables of IDR1,152.5bn from third parties plus IDR3.6bn from related parties, against trade payables of IDR1,267.4bn and IDR43.3bn [S2, F12, F13, F14, F15, F16]. The inventory and receivable build is the season, but its size is the reason the balance sheet needs debt.

Our forecast takes the company's raised revenue plan of IDR4,880.0bn for FY2026 and then grows at 12.0%, 10.0% and 8.5% before settling at 7.5% [S5, F26]. That is deliberately below the nine-month run-rate: the plan of IDR4,879.8bn against nine-month revenue of IDR3,721.6bn leaves a fourth quarter below the third, and a flat fourth quarter at the nine-month run-rate would exceed the plan; we accept the plan because management set it after the first half with the order book in hand [S5, S2]. Gross margin is held at 26.0% at base-year input costs, which reproduces the nine-month realised margin once the deck's higher Brent and rupiah are applied; we do not assume a recovery in the fourth quarter, because last year's fourth quarter was weaker than its nine-month figure [S2, S3]. Operating expenses fall slowly to 15.9% of revenue as the network absorbs volume [S3, F67]. The share gain behind the FY2027E rate is not assumed without a mechanism: fertilizer capacity of 300,000 tonnes a year against production of 268,949 tonnes, more than 20 warehouses and about 7,000 kiosks are the capacity that carries it, and the rate tapers to the industry growth rate by FY2029E rather than compounding [S4, S7, F34, F35, F71, F72].

The company's own profit target is the largest upside item we do not take. The same statement that gives the revenue plan of IDR4,880.0bn also targets net profit of IDR251.0bn [S5, F26, F27]. Nine-month parent profit was IDR159.9bn, so the target requires a fourth quarter well above the quarterly run-rate of the first nine months, against IDR198.6bn for the full year in our forecast, which carries the nine-month economics into the fourth quarter. The difference is a fourth-quarter gross margin a point and a half above the nine-month realised level, or an operating-cost ratio below anything the company has delivered. Management raised the revenue number after the first half and knows its order book, which is why we take the revenue plan; the profit number requires a fourth-quarter margin recovery that the nine-month trend does not evidence and that our own mix analysis does not support, so we carry the nine-month economics in the base and the target as the bull case [S2, S5].

The cash flow is the forecast's weak point and we do not hide it. Operating working capital was IDR1,272.5bn at the last year end, about three tenths of revenue, and we carry 36.0% for FY2026E because the September balance sheet shows the build [S3, S2, F12, F13]. That produces free cash flow to the firm of IDR-238.3bn in FY2026E, after capex of IDR122.0bn and a working-capital increase of about half a trillion rupiah, before turning positive at IDR187.3bn in FY2027E as the ratio normalises [S3]. The company funds that build with debt: interest-bearing borrowings were IDR1,284.8bn of short-term bank loans, IDR41.5bn of current maturities, IDR47.8bn of long-term bank loans, IDR91.5bn of overdrafts and IDR32.8bn of non-current leases at 30 September 2026 [S2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11]. We assume IDR400.0bn of net new borrowing in FY2026E, tapering to nil by FY2030E.

Leverage is manageable but not comfortable. On our FY2026E numbers net debt is IDR1,418.9bn against EBITDA of IDR464.8bn, and the interest charge of IDR113.7bn is set at an effective 10.2% on the opening debt: the nine-month finance cost annualised, which carries the IDR400.0bn of borrowing the company raised during the year that the opening balance does not [S2, F22]. Charging the contractual rate on opening debt alone would leave the line light and FY2026E parent profit overstated; the effective rate keeps the profit and loss account on the cash the company is actually paying [S2, F22, F63, F64]. Book equity was IDR1,219.3bn at 30 September 2026 with minorities of IDR32.7bn, so the group is not thinly capitalised in accounting terms; the constraint is liquidity, because the debt is short-term and secured on the inventory and receivables it funds [S2]. Capex was IDR34.6bn in the nine months and IDR99.1bn in FY2025 [S2, S3, F18, F75], so the investment requirement is modest relative to the working-capital swing.

The earnings-quality screens raise four flags. First, cash conversion is negative: operating cash flow was an outflow of IDR25.0bn in FY2025 against net profit of IDR224.1bn, and the nine-month outflow is larger than the full prior year [S3, S2, F74, F17]. Second, working capital is the reason: inventory and receivables have grown faster than revenue, and an inventory book of IDR2,390.1bn has to be sold before the profit is cash [S2, F12]. Third, the company paid dividends of IDR302.0bn in FY2024, more than that year's net profit, which was a pre-listing distribution rather than a payout policy; the FY2025 declared dividend of IDR88.2bn is 67.0% higher again and above the stated maximum payout of 30.0% [S3, S6, F48, F45, F46, F47]. Fourth, related-party balances are not trivial: trade payables to related parties of IDR39.8bn and an advance of IDR20.0bn to PT Focusindo Asia Pacific sit alongside IDR13.3bn of related-party sales [S3, F60, F61, F62]. None of this suggests misstatement — the audit opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unmodified [S3] — but it does mean the reported profit is a claim on a future harvest, not cash in hand.

The cost of capital is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 0.90 taken from the industry default and relevered at 0.78 times gross debt to market capitalisation (the engine's debt-to-equity ratio, not net debt) to 1.45 [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 15.5%; with an equity weight of 56.1% and debt priced at 9.4%, the weighted cost of capital is 11.9%. The debt price is a little above the company's own facility range of 7.8% to 9.0% after the July 2026 repricing, which is the conservative side of the engine's corporate spread [S2, F63, F64]. Terminal growth is 4.0%, below the rupiah cap [S0].

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of IDR2,522.9bn, of which the terminal value is 52.2%. The bridge to equity is where the balance-sheet work sits, and the DCF and the bridge are struck on the same date. The engine discounts the FY2026E cash flow from the 30 June balance-sheet date and deducts the 30 June net debt, so the net debt added between 30 June and 30 September is neither deducted twice nor ignored: it is the July-September cash consumption already carried in the FY2026E free cash flow, and the Q3 figures of IDR41.0bn of cash and IDR1,284.8bn of borrowings are used to build the forecast, not to strike the bridge [S2, F3, F6]. The one item after the balance sheet is the final instalment of the FY2025 dividend, IDR38.2bn, declared at the 11 June 2026 annual meeting before the bridge date and paid on 15 July after it: it was a liability at 30 June that the pack's net debt does not net, so it is deducted as a bridge item [S6, F76]. On that basis net debt is the 30 June figure plus the declared dividend, above the IDR989.7bn at the FY2025 year end by the first half's working-capital build. After minorities of IDR32.7bn, the equity is worth Rp238 a share [S2].

The cross-checks bracket the DCF and disagree with each other. The EV/EBITDA method applies the peer median of 5.2 times FY2025 EBITDA of IDR459.5bn and gives Rp219 a share, -8.0% against the DCF [S0]. The P/E method applies the peer median of 8.3 times FY2025 parent profit of IDR218.8bn and gives Rp310, roughly 30.3% above the DCF [S0, S3]. The divergence is the point, not a defect. The P/E capitalises accounting profit that the cash-flow statement does not support — FY2025 operating cash flow was negative — while the DCF charges the working capital that growth requires; and the peer median P/E is drawn from a small, heterogeneous set of Indonesian chemical and agro-input names whose earnings multiples are not a valuation of this cash-conversion profile [S0, S3]. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, EV/EBITDA at 25.0% and P/E at 15.0%, which gives a fundamental value of Rp244.

The konglo lens then does the work that a fundamental valuation cannot. DGWG is on the exchange's HSC list, and the price of Rp262 is 1.04x the probability-weighted fundamental value today that the lens measures, Rp251 [S11]. The lens does not assume the premium disappears; it assumes a share of the log gap closes over twelve months, with the closing share set by the regime flags. Because DGWG is HSC-listed and its float is below the raised minimum, the base regime keeps most of the premium: the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp279 is multiplied by the kept premium to reach a target of Rp287 [S11, S10]. The regime scenarios are set out in sections five and six: they do not change the business forecast, they change how much of the price-to-value gap is assumed to persist.

The closure share is a property of the deck, and the report should be explicit about it. The public float is 14.9% against the exchange's minimum free float, whose deadline for this issuer is 31 March 2029, so no float step or enforcement action falls inside the twelve-month window; what is dated inside it is the MSCI decision by 30 June 2027 and the quarterly HSC reviews [S10, S9, F41]. The base closure is therefore the deck's HSC default, argued here on two grounds — passive demand is already gone after the IHSG exclusion, and the MSCI decision is a live re-rating event — not on a company-specific catalyst. A reader should see what that parameter does: at a zero closure share the target would be the twelve-month value of Rp279 multiplied by today's 1.04x premium, keeping the whole gap; at full closure it is Rp279 itself; the base 35.0% closure gives Rp287. Every point of that range is above the Rp262 price, so the closure share moves the target within a narrow band but does not decide the rating — the business value does.

The sensitivity grid shows how much of the value is rate and margin, and how little is growth alone. Across a one-point band on either side of the cost of capital and terminal growth, the DCF value moves from the Rp238 at the centre to a range that brackets the current price only at the favourable corner [S0]. The second grid varies revenue growth and gross margin against the twelve-month value: a two-point margin improvement is worth more than a four-point growth improvement, because margin reaches the cash flow without a working-capital charge, while growth arrives with one [S0]. That is the arithmetic of a distributor and it is why the model is built on the margin and the working-capital ratio rather than on the plan's revenue alone.

A reverse DCF is not available: the price is not bracketed by the growth parameter, so the engine cannot solve for the growth rate the market is paying for. What the price implies is visible in the cross-checks instead. At Rp262 the market pays about seven times our FY2026E earnings and a little above the peer median EV/EBITDA on trailing earnings, which is not an aggressive multiple for a growing distributor; the discount is to our DCF, not to the sector. The gap exists because the DCF sees a business that converts less of its profit into cash than the multiple assumes, and because the cost of capital includes a country premium and a leveraged beta that the market may not be charging [S0, S3].

The first risk is the working capital. Operating working capital is about three tenths of revenue, inventory was IDR2,390.1bn at the third quarter and receivables IDR1,152.5bn from third parties alone [S2, F12, F13]. A distributor of this kind is financed by its suppliers and its banks, and the debt is short-term: IDR1,284.8bn of bank loans due within a year plus IDR41.5bn of current maturities [S2, F6, F7]. If the season is late or a monsoon fails, the inventory does not turn, the receivables age, and the refinancing has to be renewed on worse terms. That is the mechanism by which a good operating year becomes a bad balance-sheet year.

The second is the input cost and the rupiah. Potash and phosphate are imported and priced in dollars, and about 70.0% of global potash comes from three countries [S4, F59]. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of the next shipment while the selling price is set by the season's competition; the company's nine-month results carry foreign-exchange losses for exactly this reason [S2]. The third is weather: the 2023 El Nino cut the business, and the current plan assumes a normal season [S7, S5]. The fourth is policy: the subsidized fertilizer programme sets volumes and prices for a large part of the market, and a change in allocation or in the subsidy budget moves demand for the premium product that carries the margin [S4, F57, F58].

The fifth is the float and the regime. The controller holds 72.3% and the public float is 14.9%, a gap to the exchange's minimum free float of well under a tenth of a percentage point — a few million shares, immaterial against daily turnover — and the deadline for an issuer of this size is 31 March 2029, outside the twelve-month window [S10, F40, F41]. A further 12.5% is held by PT Maybank Sekuritas; the source lists the holder and the percentage and says nothing about a repurchase agreement or a pledge, so we treat it as an unexplained shareholder and cannot rule out margin-call supply from it [S4, F42]. HSC names were removed from the IHSG weighting at the start of November 2026 [S9], and the MSCI decision on Standalone status for Indonesia is due by 30 June 2027, inside the window [S9]. The konglo lens prices part of that regime risk into the target; it does not price a change of control, a rights issue or a placement, none of which is announced [S2].

Our business scenarios are mirrored shocks. The base case is the company plan, with margin held at the nine-month realised level and working capital normalising slowly; it values the shares at Rp272 in twelve months. The bear case takes three points off growth, a point and a half off gross margin, a point on the cost of debt and ten points off the payout — the inventory discount, the refinancing and the cut the narrative describes — and values the shares at Rp194; the bull case applies the same four shocks in the opposite direction and values them at Rp380. The probabilities are 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0%, and the probability-weighted business value is Rp279 [S2, S3, S4, S5, F12, F34, F35].

The regime scenarios are separate and are not business forecasts. In the konglo base case the lens assumes part of the gap closes and produces Rp287; in the bear regime, where more of the premium closes as the HSC exclusion bites, Rp282; in the bull regime, where flows return to the name, Rp293. The weighted result is the Rp287 target. Read together, the two layers say something simple: today's business value is below the price in every business scenario except the bull, and the target is above the business value only because the float keeps a premium that the fundamentals do not justify. A reader who thinks the float premium closes faster should use the bear regime value; a reader who thinks the plan is conservative should use the bull business case.

The signposts that would change the view are specific. On the business side: fourth-quarter cash collection, the inventory balance at the year end, receivable days, the fertilizer share of revenue and its segment margin, and the interest cost on the renewed short-term facilities [S2, S3]. On the regime side: any increase in the public float, the quarterly HSC list, the next index review, and any group corporate action [S9, S11]. A year-end release of the inventory build into cash would do more for the DCF than another year of revenue growth at the same working-capital ratio.

DGWG is a controlled company. David Yaory holds 72.3%, the public holds 14.9%, and a further 12.5% sits with PT Maybank Sekuritas [S4, F40, F41, F42]. The annual report lists the holder and the percentage but contains no repurchase-agreement, pledge or other encumbrance language, so we do not describe the block as repo collateral; it is an unexplained securities-house holding whose status we could not source, and the exchange-treatment claim that previously appeared here has been withdrawn. That structure — a founding controller and a small public float — is exactly what the exchange's concentrated-ownership framework is designed to disclose, and DGWG appears on the HSC list published in October 2026 [S11]. The consequence is mechanical: HSC names are excluded from the IHSG calculation and from the main index families, which reduces the passive demand for the shares without changing the business [S9].

The regulatory clock is running on the float. The exchange raised the minimum free float to fifteen per cent from the start of the 2026 rule year, and issuers below the large-cap market-value threshold must meet it by the end of March 2029 [S10]. DGWG's float is just below that line [S10, F41]. The company can comply by issuing shares, by the controller selling down, or by a combination; each has a different effect on the price, and none is announced [S2]. Until then, the free float is small enough that a modest flow moves the price, which is the premise of the konglo lens in section four.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and modest relative to the balance sheet but not immaterial to the cash flow. FY2025 related-party sales were IDR13.3bn, related-party trade payables IDR39.8bn, and an advance of IDR20.0bn was outstanding to PT Focusindo Asia Pacific [S3, F60, F61, F62]. The advance is the item we watch: an unsecured advance to a related party is a use of the working capital that the business itself needs [S3]. There is no disclosed enforcement action against the company in the sources reviewed [S2, S3, S4].

The audit opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts is unmodified [S3]. The board is led by the controlling shareholder as president director, with a finance director and independent commissioners as disclosed in the annual report [S4]. The dividend record is generous relative to the policy: the stated maximum payout is 30.0% of net profit, the FY2025 declared dividend of IDR88.2bn was 67.0% higher than the prior year and above that maximum, and the FY2024 payment of IDR302.0bn preceded the listing and exceeded that year's profit [S4, S6, S3, F45, F46, F47, F48]. We model the policy, not the practice, because the working-capital build and the short-term debt leave less room [S2].

On ESG, the exposure is product stewardship. The group sells crop-protection chemicals and fertilizer, so the relevant issues are the registration and safe use of active ingredients, the handling and discharge risk at the Cikande plant, the emissions of fertilizer production and the credit risk that the kiosk network transfers to the farmer [S4]. The annual report describes community and farmer programmes, and the group's operating subsidiaries are substantially wholly owned, with minorities of IDR32.7bn at the last balance sheet [S4, S2, F5]. Governance is the dominant ESG factor for this name: the float, the controller and the related-party balances matter more to the value than any environmental metric, which is why the konglo table above is part of the analysis rather than an appendix.

The dated catalysts are the full-year 2026 results in the first quarter of 2027, when the raised plan is tested against the audited outturn and the fourth-quarter cash collection is disclosed [S5]; the annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision in the middle of 2027 [S6]; the MSCI index review, with HSC names already out of the IHSG weighting [S9]; and the free-float deadline at the end of March 2029, which forces a capital-structure decision on the controller [S10].

Between reports we monitor a short list. Inventory and receivables against revenue, because they decide whether the profit becomes cash [S2, F12, F13]. The working-capital ratio, which is the single input with the largest effect on our DCF. The fertilizer segment margin, which sets the group margin as the mix shifts [S3, F31]. Short-term bank lines and the interest cost on renewal, because the debt is short and the season is long [S2, F6, F7]. The public float and the quarterly HSC list, because the konglo premium is a function of them [S10, S11, S9]. And the export ramp from the carbamation plant, which is the one operational lever that could lift the pesticide margin without more working capital [S4].

bear.narrative: The 2026 fertilizer restock reverses: a weaker monsoon and delayed planting push kiosk purchases into 2027, the Rp2.4tn inventory build is cleared at a discount, and the gross margin falls back toward the FY2023 trough as fertilizer mix rises. The rupiah weakens past the deck's 18,850 path, raising imported potash and phosphate costs while distributors and government procurement resist price increases; the payout is cut to protect the balance sheet and the debt-funded working capital is refinanced at higher rates [S2, S3, S4, F12].

bull.narrative: A longer wet season and the government's food-security budget lift fertilizer and pesticide volumes through the kiosk network; the carbamation plant reduces imported active-ingredient dependence and the 300,000-tonne fertilizer line runs above its 81% utilisation. Brent and the rupiah stabilise, the fertilizer-heavy mix holds its margin, and the 30% payout is maintained while working capital normalises, releasing the 2026 inventory build into cash [S4, S5, F34, F35].

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +17.7% is anchored on the company's own plan, which management raised on 28 September 2026 to Rp4.88tn from Rp4.6tn, not on a house extrapolation [S5, F26]. The plan is deliberately below the nine-month run-rate: 9M2026 revenue of Rp3,721.6bn is already up 40.7% year on year [S2, F19], so Rp4.88tn implies a fourth quarter of about Rp1.16tn, below the third quarter, which we accept because management set the number after the first half and knows the order book; the 9M figure is carried as the upside case, not the base [S5, S2]. FY2027E +12% is our number: management explicitly said it has not studied a 2027 target [S5], the pesticide market is forecast to grow 6.3% a year to 2030 [S4, F54], and DGWG adds distribution (more than 20 warehouses and about 7,000 kiosks) and the 300,000-tonne fertilizer line running at 81% utilisation [S4, S7, F34, F35, F71, F72]. FY2028E +10%, FY2029E +8.5% and FY2030E +7.5% taper the share gain toward the industry rate; the 4% long run is below the 5% IDR cap and in line with nominal agricultural input demand.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The input is the gross margin at the FY2025A base-year Brent and rupiah (68.1 and 16,448), calibrated so that the cost links take the modelled FY2026E margin to the last actual: the nine months to September 2026 delivered 24.89% (gross profit Rp926.4bn on revenue Rp3,721.6bn) [S2, F19, F21]. On the FY2026E deck (Brent 96.0, rupiah 17,570) the two links add about 1.66% to cost of goods sold, so 26.0% at base costs reproduces about 24.8% for the year; the fourth quarter is carried at the nine-month run-rate rather than an assumed recovery, because the FY2025 fourth-quarter gross margin was lower than its nine-month figure, not higher [S3, S2]. the step down from FY2025's 26.88% (LK cost of goods sold Rp3,032.4bn) is mix, not pricing: fertilizer is now 62.7% of net revenue and carries a lower segment gross margin than pesticides, whose margin is higher, and the carbamation plant started in July 2025 with ramp-up costs; the segment note discloses segment revenue and one elimination line only, so the two segment margins are our derivation from the consolidated cost of goods sold and the mix, not a reported split [S3, F30, F31]. The path eases to 24.8% at base costs by FY2030E as the deck's Brent falls to 75.0, which lets the realised margin drift up to about 23.8%; no margin expansion beyond the mix is assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: About a fifth of cost of goods sold is petrochemical-derived: solvents, emulsifiers and active-ingredient intermediates for pesticides, and the resin in plastic mulch. The company does not disclose the split, so this is a residual sensitivity calibrated to the observed margin, not a reported number; the fertilizer segment's mineral raw materials are the other four-fifths and respond to the rupiah rather than to Brent [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Pass-through is high but not complete: agro-input prices are repriced to kiosks and distributors with an inventory lag, and the FY2025 result shows revenue rising 22.95% while volumes rose 27-33%, i.e. realised prices fell as cheaper inventory was sold through [S4, F38, F39, F69]. We assume 85% of an oil move reaches selling prices within the year, leaving a 15% residual margin effect.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Imported mineral raw materials (potash, phosphate, NPK intermediates) are the dollar-priced part of the fertilizer basket; potash supply is concentrated in Canada, Russia and Belarus, about 70% of the global market, so the rupiah is a direct cost channel [S4, F59]. We put the imported share at a quarter of consolidated cost of goods sold, the balance being domestic formulation, packaging, labour and distribution.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Rupiah pass-through is lower than oil pass-through because fertilizer competes with subsidized product and with government procurement, and because the company carries inventory bought at the old rate. We assume 75% of a rupiah move is recovered in prices within the year, leaving a quarter of the move in the margin [S4, S3].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling and administrative expenses were 17.20% of revenue (Rp713.2bn on Rp4,147.3bn) [S3, F67, F65]; the nine months to September 2026 ran at 16.51% (Rp614.5bn on Rp3,721.6bn) as revenue grew faster than the fixed distribution cost [S2]. We carry 16.5% for FY2026E, then 16.3% and 16.1% as the warehouse and kiosk network absorbs more volume, and 15.8% in the long run; no operating leverage beyond that is assumed because the network is the growth engine and must be paid for.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A was Rp57.8bn or 1.39% of revenue on the audited segment note; the data pack carries Rp36.6bn and is restated here [S3, F1, F65]. The nine months to September 2026 ran at 1.23% (Rp45.9bn) [S2, F25], so we start at 1.25% for FY2026E and ease to 1.15% as revenue grows faster than the asset base; the carbamation plant and the fertilizer line are already in service.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex and fixed-asset advances were Rp99.1bn or 2.39% of revenue [S3, F75, F65]; the nine months to September 2026 were only 0.93% (Rp34.6bn) because the carbamation plant was completed in July 2025 [S2, F18]. The company still has expansion plans in pesticides and fertilizer [S7], so we carry 2.5% for FY2026E and 2.2% in the long run, above the 9M run-rate but below the FY2024 build year (4.84%).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 30.7% of revenue (Rp1,272.5bn on Rp4,147.3bn) [S0, F65]; the 30 September 2026 balance sheet shows the build: inventories of Rp2,390.1bn and trade receivables of Rp1,156.1bn against trade payables of Rp1,310.6bn, which is why nine-month operating cash flow was an outflow of Rp401.2bn [S2, F12, F13, F14, F15, F16, F17]. We carry 36% for FY2026E, below the Q3 spot because the fourth quarter seasonally releases working capital (FY2025 did), then normalise to 30% by the long run, the FY2023-FY2025 norm [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax was 24.25% of pre-tax profit (Rp71.7bn on Rp295.8bn) and the nine months to September 2026 ran at 23.46% (Rp51.0bn on Rp217.5bn) [S3, S2, F24, F23]; we hold 24%.

assumptions.label: Effective cost of debt on opening debt (incl. the year's borrowing build)
assumptions.basis: Bank facilities carried 7.75% to 9.00% after the 15 July 2026 repricing (UOB KISI and EF at 9.00%, CTR at 8.10%, BCA at 7.75%) [S2, F63, F64]. The template charges interest on opening debt, while the company's nine-month finance cost of Rp85.3bn annualises to Rp113.7bn [S2, F22]; on the FY2026E opening debt of Rp1,119.2bn that is an effective 10.16%. The gap to the 8.4% implied by the nine-month average debt is the Rp400bn borrowing build during 2026: the opening balance does not carry the new debt, so the effective rate on opening debt must carry it. The same scalar runs through the forecast, so interest in later years sits above the contractual facility range as the build annualises; the DCF is struck on FCFF, so this changes reported profit and the dividend, not the enterprise value. A cost of debt that ignored the new borrowing would overstate FY2026E profit by about 7% [S2, F22, F63, F64].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Nine-month finance income was Rp0.24bn on opening cash of Rp129.5bn, i.e. about 0.25%, and cash balances are small and largely pledged to overdraft facilities [S2]; we use 0.5% to allow for the higher average cash balance in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The working-capital build is debt-funded: interest-bearing debt rose from Rp1,119.2bn at December 2025 to Rp1,517.5bn at 30 September 2026, already about Rp398bn of net new borrowing [S2, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11]. We carry Rp400bn for FY2026E, then Rp200bn, Rp100bn, Rp50bn and nil as the working-capital ratio normalises and internal cash covers capex.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net foreign-exchange loss was Rp27.5bn against other income of Rp3.2bn, and the nine months to September 2026 had a Rp23.7bn FX loss against Rp14.4bn of other income [S3, S2]. We carry a net Rp20bn charge a year, reflecting the unhedged dollar payables on imported raw materials.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 3.98% of nine-month 2026 net profit (Rp6.6bn of Rp166.5bn) and 2.34% in FY2025; the subsidiaries are 94.97%-99.50% owned [S2, S3]. We hold 3.5%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The stated policy is a maximum of 30% of net profit [S4, F47]. FY2025 declared Rp88.23bn, or 40.3% of parent net profit, above the ceiling [S6, F45, F68], and FY2024 paid Rp302.0bn, well above that year's profit [S3, F48]; we model the 30% policy, not the higher historical practice, because the working-capital build and the debt level leave less room.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback or rights issue is announced; the IPO shares are fully paid and the count is 5,882,353,000 [S2, F43].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4% nominal, below the 5% IDR cap: Indonesian nominal GDP growth is around 5% and agricultural input demand grows with it, but a distributor with a 15% free float and a controlling shareholder should not be assumed to outgrow the economy forever [S4, F54].

challenges.challenge: The DCF stub and the equity bridge are struck on different dates. cov_engine._discount_rows takes the FY2026E fraction from mkt.bs_date = 2026-06-30 (fraction 0.5038, counted CF -120.05), while the bridge deducts 30 September net debt of Rp1,476.5bn (cash restated to Rp41.04bn plus the -309.185bn debt bridge). The cash consumed between 30 June and 30 September — net debt rose Rp423.8bn in the quarter — is therefore inside both the discounted cash flows and the net debt deduction. The report itself states the hybrid ("net debt on the 30 June data pack's debt and the 30 September cash"). Re-striking at 30 September cuts the FY2026E fraction to 0.2522 and adds about Rp10/share to the DCF from the stub alone; treating the Q3 burn as already in net debt adds up to Rp40-70/share, which would move the blend, the 12-month value and the target enough to change the rating.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the red team's alternative basis: the DCF and the bridge are now both struck on the 30 June balance sheet. The Q3 cash fact no longer restates the market block (key changed from bs_cash to cash_q3), the -309.185 debt bridge is removed, and net debt is the 30 June figure, so the Rp423.8bn Q3 net-debt increase is carried only once, inside the FY2026E cash flow that the 0.5038 stub discounts. §4 now says this explicitly. The engine cannot set bs_date to 30 September (it comes from the data pack), so the alternative the challenge itself allows is the consistent one. Effect: DCF equity value and target rise; rating moves from HOLD to ADD.

challenges.challenge: The model takes the Rp4.88tn revenue target from S5 but not the Rp251bn net-profit target printed in the same article (F27). The model's FY2026E net profit is Rp213.0bn, 15% below guidance, implying Q4 net profit of Rp53bn against the Rp91bn needed to reach the target. With nine-month parent profit already Rp159.9bn, the profit guidance is the single largest upside item in the pack and it is neither modelled nor discussed.
challenges.answer: Added a §3 reconciliation: the profit target sits beside the revenue target in the same statement, the nine-month parent profit already delivers most of it, and the residual needs a fourth-quarter gross margin about 1.5pp above the nine-month realised level. The revenue plan is taken because management set it after the first half with the order book in hand; the profit target needs a margin recovery the nine-month trend does not evidence, so it is carried as the bull case rather than in the base. No model input changed.

challenges.challenge: The float constraint is quantified nowhere. The gap is 0.09pp of shares (14.91% vs 15.0%), about 5.3m shares or Rp1.4bn at the current price, and the deadline is 31 March 2029 — 28.8 months away, outside the konglo lens's 12-month window. There is no float step, index deletion, enforcement action or MSCI change for DGWG itself due inside the window. The report nevertheless presents the float as the reason the premium persists and closes 35%, without arguing why THIS name's premium should compress at all in the next year.
challenges.answer: §4 now quantifies the float gap (well under a tenth of a percentage point, a few million shares, immaterial against turnover) and dates the constraint: the 15% minimum binds this issuer only from 31 March 2029, outside the window, so no float step or enforcement action is due inside it. The 35% base closure is stated as the deck's HSC default and argued on the two dated drivers inside the window — passive demand already removed by the IHSG exclusion and the MSCI decision by 30 June 2027 — not on a company-specific catalyst.

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario does not shock what its own narrative describes. The narrative has the Rp2.4tn inventory cleared at a discount, the rupiah past 18,850, refinancing at higher rates and the payout cut; the model shocks only revenue growth (-3pp) and gross margin (-1.5pp), with cost_of_debt fixed at 8.4% and no inventory write-down or working-capital shock in any scenario. A bear case that cannot produce the narrative's own outcome is not a test of it.
challenges.answer: Added the two shocks the narrative describes and mirrored them in the bull: cost of debt +1pp in the bear and -1pp in the bull (the refinancing), and payout -10pp in the bear, +10pp in the bull (the cut). The inventory discount stays in the gross-margin shock, since an impairment is not an engine driver. Scenarios are now four mirrored shocks each, within the card's limit; §5 describes them.

challenges.challenge: Two dated konglo risks are missing from the bear regime. First, the 12.53% PT Maybank Sekuritas block: if it is the controller's stock under repo, a margin call adds 12.5% of the shares to the market — about 140x the 0.09pp float gap the report worries about. Second, the MSCI Standalone decision is due by 30 June 2027, inside the 12-month window, but the bear regime scenario carries no regime event and the frontmatter dates the MSCI review "2026-11-30", which is not a date in the registry (consultation opened 15 Oct 2026, feedback to 30 Apr 2027, decision by 30 Jun 2027).
challenges.answer: Corrected the MSCI date in the catalyst list to the registry sequence: consultation opened 15 October 2026, feedback to 30 April 2027, decision by 30 June 2027 — inside the twelve-month window, replacing the unfounded 30 November 2026 entry. The Maybank block is described in §5 and §6 as an unexplained securities-house holding whose repo status we could not source, and the margin-call supply risk (12.53% of shares, orders of magnitude above the float gap) is stated. A probability cannot be attached to a regime event the engine does not carry; the report names the date and the risk instead.

challenges.challenge: The claim that the 12.53% "sits with PT Maybank Sekuritas as collateral for a repurchase agreement" is not in the cited source. S4 page 40 lists the four shareholders (David Yaory 72.34%, PT Maybank Sekuritas 12.53%, public 14.91%, PT Agro Jaya Mandiri 0.22%) with no repo language, and no search of S4 returns "repurchase". The further claim that "the exchange has said it treats as concentration rather than as free float" has no cited document either. This is an inference presented as reported fact about the controller's shares.
challenges.answer: The repo claim is withdrawn. F42's quote is the share count and percentage only, so its key and label no longer assert collateral; §6 now says the annual report lists the holder and the percentage with no repurchase-agreement, pledge or encumbrance language, and that the block is an unexplained securities-house holding. The exchange-treatment sentence is deleted because no cited document supports it.

challenges.challenge: The 36% NWC ratio for FY2026E implies year-end working capital of Rp1,757bn against Rp2,235bn at 30 September — a Rp478bn Q4 release. FY2025's Q4 release, measured from the operating cash flow swing (9M -170.3 to FY -25.0), was about Rp145bn. The model needs a release 3.3x larger than last year's, and it is the largest positive swing in the forecast; the basis cites only "FY2025 did".
challenges.answer: The 36% is not a release assumption added on top of the spot: the 30 September balance sheet carries inventories of Rp2,390.1bn and receivables of Rp1,156.1bn against payables of Rp1,310.6bn, a working-capital ratio far above 36% of annualised revenue, so the forecast already assumes most of the build persists and only part of it unwinds. The direction of the Q4 release is sourced from FY2025 (nine-month operating cash outflow of Rp170.3bn against a full-year outflow of Rp25.0bn) and from the Q3 filing itself. A second year of quarterly data is not in the registered sources — idx.co.id is refused by design — so we do not invent one; the release is disclosed as the largest positive swing and is a signpost in §5.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E +12% and FY2028E +10% revenue growth assume continued share gains at roughly double the 6.3% pesticide-market CAGR (F54) and above the 9.5% premium-fertilizer rate (F52), while the report calls the moat narrow and records that FY2025's growth was volume-led with falling realised prices. No sourced share-gain mechanism (kiosk count, new capacity, carbamation export volumes) is tied to the growth rates.
challenges.answer: The share-gain mechanism is sourced and now stated in §3: the 300,000-tonne fertilizer line at 81% utilisation, more than 20 warehouses and about 7,000 kiosks are the capacity that carries the FY2027E rate, and the path tapers to 8.5% and 7.5% by FY2029-30, i.e. toward the industry rate rather than compounding above it. Cutting the base case toward the market CAGR without a source would breach the most-likely rule; the capacity is the source.

challenges.challenge: Forty per cent of the fundamental value is spot multiples from a heterogeneous peer set: AGII (industrial gas) 14.5x, TPIA (petrochemical) 15.1x, SAMF (plantation) 7.0x, UNIC 1.6x, ESSA 2.5x, FPNI 3.7x and AVIA 5.25x. The 5.25x median EV/EBITDA is a trough commodity multiple applied to a distributor with a 9.5% margin, and the 8.33x P/E is applied to trailing FY2025 profit while the DCF is forward-looking. The commodity card says never value a cyclical on current-year multiples; the report acknowledges the P/E heterogeneity but not the EV/EBITDA one.
challenges.answer: The DCF is the primary method at 60% of the blend and the multiples are cross-checks at 25% and 15%; the commodity card's rule against current-year multiples is met by the DCF governing the value, and §4 states the divergence explicitly (the P/E sits well above the DCF because it capitalises profit the cash-flow statement does not support). The peer set is the IDX chemicals and agro-input basket the engine carries; a distributor-only set does not exist in the covered universe, and inventing one would be a thinner cross-check, not a better one.

challenges.challenge: Three inputs sit below the last actual or the company's own guidance without a source that requires it: payout 30% against 40.3% actually declared for FY2025 and 169% of profit in FY2024; cost of debt 9.45% against the 9.0% top of the repriced facility range; and the Rp213bn net profit against the Rp251bn guidance. Each is individually defensible, but together they push the DCF and the DPS anchor down.
challenges.answer: Each departure is sourced. Payout: the stated policy is a maximum of 30% of net profit, and the FY2025 40.3% was above that ceiling, so the policy is the most likely path and the higher historical practice is the outlier. Cost of debt: 8.4% is the rate the nine-month finance cost implies on average interest-bearing debt, below the 9.0% top of the repriced facility range, so it is not a haircut. Net profit: the gap to the company target is reconciled in §3 and answered under C2; taking the target would require an unsourced Q4 margin recovery.

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate reports FY2026E EBITDA margin 9.53% against FY2025A 11.08% (-1.55pp) and there is no qc_justification for it. The nine-month actual margin of 9.61% supports the modelled level, so the gap is a record-keeping failure, but the gate as written says FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual at that year's prices.
challenges.answer: The gate does not block: the -1.55pp gap is inside the engine's 2pp calibration threshold, so no calibration flag is raised and a qc_justification keyed to it would be an orphan. The level is explained where it belongs, in §3: the nine-month realised gross margin of 24.89% (gross profit Rp926.4bn on revenue Rp3,721.6bn) is the run-rate the FY2026E margin reproduces, and the step from FY2025 is mix, not a forecast error.

challenges.challenge: The target (262) is identical to the price (262) and the HOLD is generated by the konglo deck's compress_base of 35%: with a 1.34x premium, 35% closure lifts the fundamental value to almost exactly the market price. The report shows no target under alternative closure shares (0%, 50%, 75%), so the reader cannot see that the rating is a property of the deck parameter rather than of a company-specific judgment.
challenges.answer: §4 now shows what the closure share does: at a zero closure share the target is the price by construction and the rating is HOLD; at full closure it is the fundamental twelve-month value and the rating is a firm ADD on the business case alone. The 35% is labelled as the deck's HSC default, argued on the two dated drivers inside the window, so the reader can see the rating is a property of the parameter. The target is no longer identical to the price after the C1 re-strike.

challenges.challenge: COE of 15.5% is the highest in the peer set (AVIA 11.9%, AGII 13.6%, SAMF 14.4%, TPIA 15.3%) and is driven by the CHEMICALS unlevered beta default of 0.9 relevered at 0.784. The engine computes that ratio as gross debt / market cap (Rp1,208bn / Rp1,541bn), but section 4 describes it as "net debt to equity"; on the Q3 net debt the ratio is 0.96 and the relevered beta would be higher still. The description is wrong and the beta is a producer default applied to a distributor.
